verdict.reasoning: Patient reports wheeze and shortness of breath: 'She's feeling a little bit wheezy.' and 'I'm feeling, like, a little bit short of breath.'

She links onset to dust exposure during house cleaning two days ago: 'it started, like, about two days ago... cleaning the house and, like, all this dust came out of the carpet' and 'two days later. Still not gotten any better'. Shortness of breath is described in the same context.
'Did the wheezing start suddenly or was it gradual?' / Patient: 'So it started after maybe an hour or so.'—referring to after the cleaning/dust exposure.
She indicates symptoms have continued: 'two days later. Still not gotten any better' implying persistence of wheeze/shortness of breath.
Patient: 'Yeah, so it gets a bit worse at night, I find.' referring to the wheeze.

Intermittent pattern of wheeze (coming and going) is not described; transcript only notes continuous symptoms worsening at night: 'two days later. Still not gotten any better' and 'it gets a bit worse at night'.
Intermittent shortness of breath is not explicitly stated; she reports being 'a little bit short of breath' but does not describe it as intermittent.
Speech-limiting dyspnea is described: 'when I'm, you know, talking to my friends and stuff, finding that sometimes I'm unable to complete my sentences, it can get really bad.'
She denies pain with deep breath (pleuritic pain): Doctor: 'when you can breathe and you take a deep breath, do you notice any pain?' Patient: 'No, no. No pain.'
Doctor asks about dizziness and she denies: 'have you noticed yourself feeling dizzy or the room spinning more than normal?' Patient: 'No, no dizziness? None of that.'
Patient: 'Yeah, yeah, I think I'm having, like, you know, four or five glasses a day.' referring to drinking water.
Doctor: 'But you don't see your doctor regularly for asthma?' Patient: 'No, I don't.'
Patient volunteers: 'I mean, I have before taken steroids for asthma. I don't know if that's relevant.'
Patient: 'I used to have, like, a bit of asthma as a child.'

She describes exertional asthma symptoms: 'sometimes when I run for, like, long periods, it can. It can start up a bit, but I have, like, an asthma inhaler.' This indicates exertion-triggered intermittent asthma.
Patient: 'also in the summer, I sometimes get hay fever.' which is seasonal allergic rhinitis.
Regarding inhaler: Doctor: 'So do you still have your inhalers?' Patient: 'I think I might have one from like a couple of months ago.'
Doctor: 'have you taken anything for the wheeze?' Patient: 'No. No, I haven't, actually.'
Doctor: 'apart from this, do you know if you're allergic to anything?' Patient: 'Not that I know of.' which corresponds to no known allergies.

All components are present: acute 2‑day wheeze/SOB after dust ('it started... about two days ago... all this dust came out'), history of asthma/hay fever, worse at night ('it gets a bit worse at night'), speech-limiting dyspnea ('sometimes I'm unable to complete my sentences'), and no pleuritic pain or dizziness ('No, no. No pain.' and 'No, no dizziness? None of that.').
Doctor: 'given you've got a history of asthma and hay fever, this could be one of two things, but we want to rule out asthma or an allergy first.' indicating asthma exacerbation vs allergic reaction.

Doctor: 'what you need is visit one of our clinics so we can do some more tests' and later 'The consultation with the GP in person shouldn't take too long.' indicating in-person GP/clinic evaluation planned imminently.

Doctor: 'the first thing we would do is use a small device on your finger to check the amount of oxygen in your blood.' and 'so we can do some more tests.'—this is fingertip oximetry plus further testing as indicated.

Doctor: 'if you've got something like an antihistamine, which you normally take for hay fever at home, I would take one just in case it is an allergy... You might be able to get one on your way to the doctor's surgery.'
Doctor: 'If not, they can prescribe you one.' referring to the GP prescribing an antihistamine if not obtained OTC.
Doctor: 'you may need to take some steroids now. But we cannot, we won't be able to know until we've done those tests first.' indicating steroids will be considered if indicated after evaluation.

Doctor: 'I'm going to write a letter for your GP just to let him know what's happened.' and 'You should get the letter over the app and then we can. You can take yourself to the gp. ... The consultation with the GP in person shouldn't take too long. ... Probably 10 minutes.'
